title: Graph Theory Fundamentals
blurb: Tests BFS against DFS, unweighted shortest paths against Dijkstra, degree, betweenness and PageRank as three different meanings of importance, Louvain community detection and modularity, and what the service graph and karate club showed.

questions.prompt: Why does BFS find a fewest-hops path?
options: It searches every possible path and keeps the shortest.
It goes layer by layer, so first arrival is shortest.
It uses a stack, which favours short paths.
It always follows the edge with the lowest weight.
questions.explanation: With a queue, all one-hop nodes come before two-hop ones. DFS uses a stack and follows one chain deeply first.

refLinks.label: §76.2.1 BFS vs. DFS: Two Different Discovery Orders, Not Two Ways to the Same Answer

questions.prompt: How should you choose between BFS and DFS?
options: By edge weights, since DFS handles weighted edges.
By the question asked. Both are O(V + E).
By graph size, since BFS fails on large graphs.
By speed, since DFS is always faster.
questions.explanation: BFS suits "minimum hops to X". DFS suits tracing one dependency chain end to end. Their cost is the same.

questions.prompt: What does nx.dijkstra_path minimise that nx.shortest_path doesn't?
options: The degree of the nodes on the route
The number of nodes visited during the search
The number of hops along the route
The sum of edge weights along the route
questions.explanation: shortest_path counts every edge as one hop. Dijkstra adds up real costs such as latency.

refLinks.label: §76.2.2 Shortest Path: Hops Are Not Cost

questions.prompt: Two 2-hop routes run from api_gateway to database: via user_service (8 ms, then 12 ms) and via auth_service (5 ms, then 10 ms). What latency does Dijkstra's path have, in ms?
questions.explanation: The auth_service route costs 5 + 10 = 15 ms against 8 + 12 = 20 ms. Same hops, different cost.

questions.prompt: Some edge costs are negative, such as a rebate. What does the chapter say to use?
options: PageRank, since it handles negative edges
Dijkstra, after taking absolute values of the weights
Bellman-Ford, since Dijkstra needs weights ≥ 0
BFS, since it ignores weights entirely
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy choice is only correct with non-negative weights, and it fails silently otherwise. Bellman-Ford is slower but correct.

options: How many direct neighbours a node has
The share of shortest paths passing through a node
How much importance flows in from important nodes linking to it
How densely a node's neighbours connect to each other
questions.explanation: High betweenness means traffic has no way around you. Neighbour count is degree. Importance from important neighbours is PageRank.

refLinks.label: §76.2.3 Centrality: Three Measures, Three Different Definitions of “Important”

questions.prompt: In a 9-node graph, a node has 5 neighbours. What is its degree centrality, normalised by n − 1?
questions.explanation: 5 / (9 − 1) = 0.625, the value order_service and database shared in the worked example.

refLinks.label: §76.2.3 Centrality: Three Measures, Three Different Definitions of “Important”

questions.prompt: Why did database have the highest PageRank (0.340) but zero betweenness?
options: It is isolated from the rest of the graph.
It has the fewest connections of any node.
It's a sink: depended on, never passed through.
Betweenness can't be computed on directed graphs.
questions.explanation: Nothing calls out of it, so it never lies between two other services. "Everything depends on me" and "no way around me" are different claims.

questions.prompt: A customer asks for their single point of failure. What does the chapter suggest you give them?
options: Only the node with the highest degree
The node with the most edges to the database
Both the top-PageRank and top-betweenness nodes
Only the node with the highest PageRank
questions.explanation: Losing a heavily depended-on sink and losing a structural bottleneck break the system for different reasons. Degree alone tied the two key nodes.

refLinks.label: §76.2.3 Centrality: Three Measures, Three Different Definitions of “Important”

questions.prompt: What does Louvain community detection maximise?
options: Modularity, density beyond random
Accuracy against known group labels
The betweenness of the boundary nodes
The number of communities found
questions.explanation: It uses only the edges, no labels. Checking against ground truth is a separate step.

refLinks.label: §76.2.4 Community Detection: Structure Alone, Checked Against Ground Truth

questions.prompt: With no ground truth, how can you sanity-check communities, per Procedure 76.4?
options: Check that exactly two communities were found.
You can't. Without labels, any result is meaningless.
Check that every community has the same size.
Check modularity, roughly above 0.3.
questions.explanation: Modularity near zero means the groups aren't denser than random. The algorithm can't know the "right" count.

questions.prompt: When should you use a DiGraph instead of a Graph?
options: When edges carry weights
When the graph has more than 1,000 nodes
When relationships have a direction that matters
When relationships are symmetric, such as friendship
questions.explanation: DiGraph for one-way relationships, Graph for symmetric ones. Weights work in both.

questions.prompt: Louvain matched the real karate-club split for 33 of 34 members. What percentage is that? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: 33 / 34 = 0.971, from structure alone with no faction labels.

questions.prompt: Louvain found 4 communities, though the club split into 2 factions. How was agreement still 97%?
options: Each of the 4 groups sat inside one of the 2 factions.
Louvain was told to merge communities into two at the end.
The factions were redefined to match the communities.
The two extra communities were ignored in the count.
questions.explanation: agreement_with_ground_truth labels each community by its majority. Finer structure can still respect the real split.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain, in your own words, why BFS is guaranteed to find a fewest-hops path the first time it reaches a node, using the queue-based mechanism described in the Exposition.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: BFS explores nodes in strict order of increasing distance from the source, using a queue that processes all nodes at distance $k$ before adding any at distance $k+1$. So by the time a node is first dequeued (reached), every shorter possible path to it has already been exhausted without success, guaranteeing the path found is the fewest-hops path.

bookExercises.prompt: State the practical difference between degree centrality, betweenness centrality, and PageRank in one sentence each, without using the word "important."
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Degree centrality: how many direct connections a node has. Betweenness centrality: how much shortest-path traffic between *other* node pairs flows through this node. PageRank: how much a node is linked to by other well-linked nodes, recursively.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 76.2, compute the fewest-hops path and the Dijkstra path from `api_gateway` to `payment_service` on this chapter's microservice graph, and state whether they agree on both hop count and route.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Answer depends on the specific microservice graph's structure and weights as defined in the chapter. The mechanical step is running `nx.shortest_path` (unweighted, fewest-hops) and `nx.dijkstra_path` (weighted) between `api_gateway` and `payment_service` and comparing both the hop count and the actual node sequence. They agree when the fewest-hops route also happens to be the cheapest-weighted route; they can diverge when a longer-hop-count path has lower total edge weight than a shorter one.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 76.3's output table, identify which single-node failure would be most damaging by betweenness centrality alone, and explain in one sentence why that answer differs from the highest-PageRank node.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The most damaging single-node failure by betweenness centrality alone is whichever node the output table ranks highest on that specific column, typically a node sitting on many shortest paths between otherwise-disconnected parts of the graph (a structural bridge/bottleneck). This can differ from the highest-PageRank node because PageRank rewards being linked *to* by important nodes (an endpoint of importance), while betweenness rewards sitting *between* other nodes on their shortest paths (a routing bottleneck). A node can be a critical routing chokepoint without itself being heavily linked-to, and vice versa.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 76.4, re-run Louvain community detection on the karate club graph with a different `seed` value, and describe whether the *number* of communities or their *membership* is more likely to change, based on this chapter's discussion of Louvain's stochastic step.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Per this chapter's discussion of Louvain's stochastic step, re-running with a different `seed` is more likely to change community *membership* (which specific nodes land in which cluster, especially borderline nodes) than the overall *number* of communities detected. Louvain's greedy local-optimization order is randomized by seed, which can shift ambiguous nodes between adjacent communities, while the broader structural division into roughly that many communities tends to be more stable across seeds for a graph with reasonably clear community structure.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer asks, "what's our single point of failure?" about a service architecture. Using this chapter's `database`-vs-`order_service` distinction, write the two or three sentences you'd say back, including why the answer isn't a single node.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "There typically isn't one single point of failure. A `database` node failing usually means direct, catastrophic data-layer outage, while an `order_service` node with high betweenness centrality failing disrupts many *paths* between other services without necessarily being the most-connected node itself. The honest answer depends on which failure mode you're actually worried about: direct dependency loss (check degree/direct connections) versus routing disruption (check betweenness). Worth computing both before naming one node."

bookExercises.prompt: A customer's graph has 50 million edges and needs to be queried by three different internal applications simultaneously. Using this chapter's Trade-offs section and AWS Neptune note, write the recommendation you'd give, including what would change your answer if the graph were 5,000 edges and queried by one internal script.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "At 50 million edges queried by three concurrent applications, Amazon Neptune (managed, scales past in-memory limits, handles concurrent query load) is the right recommendation over in-memory networkx, which won't hold a graph that size and has no built-in concurrency handling. If the graph were instead 5,000 edges queried by one internal script, in-memory networkx is simpler, cheaper, and sufficient. The crossover is really about scale (fits in memory?) and concurrent access needs (multiple simultaneous querying applications?), not an inherent superiority of either approach."

bookExercises.prompt: Read the Zachary 1977 paper's description of the karate club dispute. Identify the one member this chapter's Worked Example flags as a mismatch between the detected communities and the real split, and propose one plausible real-world reason (not visible from the graph structure alone) that member might have been genuinely ambiguous.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. The chapter's Worked Example flags one specific karate-club member (historically member 9 in most published analyses of this dataset) as a case where the algorithmically-detected community assignment disagrees with the real-world club split Zachary recorded. A plausible real-world explanation not visible from graph structure alone: that member may have had genuine social or logistical ties pulling toward one faction (e.g. friendship, geographic proximity) while formally affiliating with the other faction for unrelated reasons (e.g. deference to the instructor, administrative convenience), exactly the kind of context edges in a pure interaction graph can't encode.
